methodological_rigor.justification: Two complementary retrospective analyses using the large Flatiron Health EHR database provide real-world evidence with substantial sample sizes (3170 for utilization; 6350 for outcomes). Multivariable logistic regression for utilization and Cox proportional hazards models for outcomes with appropriate adjustment factors are methodological strengths. Key limitations include: over 50% missing Ki-67 data potentially misclassifying N1/N1mi patients, inability to capture patient comorbidities and shared decision-making factors, and different time origins for HR+ and eTNBC outcome comparisons (sensitivity analyses mitigated this). The Flatiron database is EHR-derived and subject to documentation heterogeneity.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This study directly addresses a critical real-world implementation gap for an FDA-approved treatment with established OS benefit. The finding that 60% of eligible patients did not receive abemaciclib, with N1/N1mi patients most undertreated (69.1%), has immediate implications for clinical practice and oncologist education. Demonstrating that N+ high-risk patients on ET alone have similar 5-year recurrence risk to TNBC (29.1% vs 25.7%) powerfully contextualizes the treatment gap. The large real-world US multi-institutional cohort provides practice-informing evidence beyond what is captured in clinical trials.

reporting_quality.justification: Patient attrition is documented in supplementary figures, Kaplan-Meier curves are provided for IDFS, DRFS, and OS, and multivariable models include appropriate covariates. The two-study design with separate cohorts and different Flatiron datasets is clearly explained. Key limitations include the retrospective Flatiron database design with inherent EHR documentation variability. Patient-level data are not publicly available due to commercial database restrictions. The missing Ki-67 data issue is acknowledged but the magnitude of its potential impact on primary findings is not fully quantified.

novelty_literature.justification: Real-world abemaciclib utilization studies exist (Sheffield et al., Rajendran et al. referenced in the paper), but this study provides the most comprehensive multi-institutional analysis with both utilization and outcome data in a contemporary cohort. The side-by-side comparison of N+ high-risk and eTNBC outcomes with matched follow-up is a novel framing that directly motivates the treatment gap narrative. The nodal subgroup outcome analysis (N1/N1mi vs N2 vs N3) provides additional granularity not previously characterized in real-world data.

writing_presentation.justification: Clearly structured with two distinct study designs presented sequentially and transparently. The clinical message is effectively communicated: the treatment gap is quantified, the risk stakes are contextualized, and actionable guidance is offered in the conclusions. Multiple Kaplan-Meier figures for different outcome measures are well-organized. Limitations are comprehensively and honestly discussed. Minor issue: the two-study design with different Flatiron subsets could be presented more clearly to avoid reader confusion.

key_strengths: Large real-world US multi-institutional cohort (n=3170 for utilization) identifying a 60% treatment gap for an FDA-approved agent with proven OS benefit
Novel comparison of N+ high-risk HR+ EBC outcomes to eTNBC showing equivalent recurrence risk (29.1% vs 25.7% at 5 years), powerfully motivating treatment intensification
Nodal subgroup outcome analysis demonstrating that N1/N1mi high-risk patients have nearly double the 5-year recurrence risk of N1/N1mi non-high-risk (14.3% absolute difference in IDFS)
Multivariable analyses with appropriate covariate adjustment and multiple outcome endpoints (IDFS, DRFS, OS) with sensitivity analyses
key_concerns: Over 50% missing Ki-67 data in Study 2 may misclassify N1/N1mi patients as non-high-risk, biasing relative risk estimates in the primary comparison
Inability to capture clinical comorbidities, patient preferences, and physician-patient discussions limits interpretation of utilization patterns as avoidable treatment gaps
Different time origins for HR+ and eTNBC outcome analyses (ET initiation vs chemotherapy initiation) introduce residual bias despite sensitivity analyses
Commercial database restrictions prevent independent data access; study was industry-sponsored (Eli Lilly), which may influence framing of findings
chief_reviewer.rationale: This pragmatic real-world study provides actionable evidence on abemaciclib underutilization and documents high recurrence risk in N+ high-risk EBC comparable to TNBC, with sufficient sample size and appropriate methodology for Tier 3 publication; the industry sponsorship and missing data limitations should be addressed in revisions.
